summary: An April 1st humorous memo about handing out IP numbers on temporary field networks and small events. It is a joke and not a real protocol, though it pokes fun at the practical problems of running such networks.

plainLanguage.summary: A joke about handing out numbered name tags to computers at a small event, without anyone really in charge.

questions: april fools rfc ip address allocation
subtitle: A humorous protocol for handing out IP addresses using wooden clothespegs

tldr.problem: Temporary field networks at large events where many computers arrive and need IP addresses quickly have no clear organizational infrastructure and cannot rely on traditional DHCP servers, which may not work with all systems present.
tldr.mechanism: This April Fools RFC humorously proposes peg-dhcp: a low-tech protocol using wooden clothespegs. Each peg is labeled with an IP address or network range. Pegs are clipped to a clothesline (the repository) and handed out by a server person to clients who visit in person. Clients read the information from the peg and manually configure their computers. A paper note lists shared configuration (netmask, gateway, proxy).
tldr.outcome: This is an April Fools joke, though it is grounded in a real experience at the HIP97 (Hacking In Progress) event where peg-dhcp was actually used. The memo describes the practical benefits (cheap, visible status, easy to track) but also its limitations (human error, potential for misconfiguration, no automatic recovery).

today: RFC 2322 is an April Fools joke RFC. However, the peg-dhcp protocol was actually implemented at the HIP97 event in 1997 and worked as described. The RFC memorializes a creative practical solution to a real problem in network administration and remains a celebrated example of an RFC that started as a joke but has elements grounded in lived experience.

sections.title: The Problem and Solution
sections.content: This RFC describes peg-dhcp, a humorous protocol for assigning IP addresses at field networks and large temporary events that lack a clear organizational structure. The problem was first addressed at the HIP event (Hacking In Progress), a large three-day event where over a thousand hackers gathered from around the world and brought computers needing TCP/IP network access. A software solution like a traditional DHCP server was judged impractical due to the variety of operating systems and IP stacks present. Instead, the organizers devised a physical solution using wooden clothespegs. Each peg represents one IP address or network block, is labeled with the IP number in text, and can be clipped to a network cable to show which computer uses which address.
sections.plainLanguage: At a big hacker party, many people brought computers needing network setup. Instead of running software, they used wooden clothespegs labeled with IP addresses.

sections.title: The Peg-DHCP Server and Client
sections.content: The server location can be a central tent (at HIP97) or a small table in a terminal room. The server hands out two items: the peg itself, labeled with an IP address or network block, and optional additional papers with fixed configuration (netmask, gateway, proxy) for the entire site. The peg can show a single IP (written as num.num.num.num, num.num, or num), or a network block (written as num.num.num/mask). Pegs are stored on a clothesline, organized by subnet, with different colored pegs for different subnets. On the client side, the person reads the information from the peg and the paper, then manually enters the configuration into the computer's IP settings. The memo notes that this human transfer of information is not error-free and that network knowledge is required from the person doing configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone runs a table where computers can pick up pegs. The peg says the computer's IP address. The person using the computer reads it and types the address into their system. Colors show different networks.

sections.title: Reclamation, Reuse, and Extensions
sections.content: When a client no longer needs an IP address, they can return the peg to the server for reuse. If the server is unmanned, clients place pegs back into the pool themselves. The memo describes extensions such as using different colored pegs for subnets, printing multiple copies of the configuration paper for mass distribution, and even theoretically combining peg-dhcp with RFC 1149 (IP datagrams on avian carriers) by attaching pegs to the leg of a carrier pigeon. The memo notes that TTL implementation is difficult; one obvious TTL is the end of the event. The final section notes that pegs are small and can be lost, but once clipped to a network cable the risk is minimized, and all information is in plain text and readable to everyone, so private information should not be exchanged through this protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: When you are done with your peg, you return it for someone else to use. You can make pegs in different colors for different networks. Everything is visible and in plain text, so do not send secrets through it.

references.text: Waitzman, D., "Transmission of IP Datagrams on Avian Carriers", RFC 1149, April 1990.
